extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers interested in fiction/novel characterization
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and developing novel characters using E.M. Forster's distinction between 'round' and 'flat' characters, situated within his seven 'aspects' of the novel. Useful for novelists seeking principles for character depth and for readers/critics assessing character quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that 'function all round' — more highly organized, able to meet greater plot demands, and 'ready for an extended life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim guidance from Forster quoted in the post: 'Why do the characters in Jane Austen give us a slightly new pleasure each time they come in, as opposed to the merely repetitive pleasure that is caused by a character in Dickens? … [T]he best reply is that her characters though smaller than his are more highly organized. They function all round, and even if her plot made greater demands on them than it does, they would still be adequate. … All the Jane Austen characters are ready for an extended life, for a life which the scheme of her books seldom requires them to lead, and that is why they lead their lives so satisfactorily.' Practical implication: create characters with enough internal organization and range that they would remain believable and interesting under different plot demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that produce 'merely repetitive pleasure' and lack the fullness or organization of 'round' characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As implied by Forster's contrast (using Dickens as an example), flat characters are limited in scope and do not provide new pleasures on repeated appearances. The blog author notes that 'flat' is often used as a critical trope in reader reviews; Forster's explanation offers guidance for avoiding this by making characters more 'highly organized' and 'ready for an extended life.'
